input.title: India AI Rules: What Is Law and What Is Expected?
input.dek: India’s 2026 IT Rules cover specified synthetic media. Here is what is in force, how the takedown clocks differ, and what remains only an expectation.
input.author: global-ai-news-editorial-desk
input.body:
The bottom line India’s current framework and its next policy step are different things. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 were notified on 10 February and came into force on 20 February. They add due-diligence duties for intermediaries concerning specified synthetic audio, visual and audiovisual information. A separate consultation paper on broader AI governance was described by the IT minister as forthcoming in October and later as arriving “in the coming weeks,” according to two news reports. As of this draft’s 31 October check, we did not locate that paper on the official sources searched. The timetable is not itself a rule, and a consultation paper—if issued—would not automatically be binding law. Key facts at a glance The 2026 amendment is a change to the existing IT Rules, not a standalone AI Act. [1][2] SGI is defined around specified realistic audio, visual or audiovisual information—not every use of AI. [1] The Gazette text includes ordinary good-faith edits and accessibility improvements among exclusions, subject to the specific conditions in the rule. [1] A three-hour period relates to specified removal action after a qualifying government or court intimation—not a universal deadline for every AI-generated post. [1][3] The minister’s reported consultation-paper timetable is an expectation attributed to him, not a statutory deadline. [7][8] Timeline: what changed, and what is still expected Date — Event — Status 22 October 2025 — MeitY published a draft amendment and explanatory note on synthetic information. — Proposal for consultation, not the final rule. [5][6] 10 February 2026 — The government notified G.S.R. 120(E), amending the IT Rules, 2021. — Binding notification. [1] 20 February 2026 — The amendment came into force. — In force. [1] 30 July 2026 — PIB summarized the SGI framework and specified shorter response timelines. — Government explanation; the Gazette controls legal wording. [3] 8 October 2026 — News on AIR reported the minister expected a broader AI-governance consultation paper within about a month. — Attributed statement. [7] 26 October 2026 — MediaNama reported the minister later said the paper would come “in the coming weeks.” — Attributed statement. [8] 31 October 2026 — This research check found no official consultation paper in the MeitY materials reviewed. — Search result, not proof that no document exists elsewhere. Original visuals Status map: law, explanation and expectation
View data Item — Status at 31 October 2026 — Evidence G.S.R. 120(E) amendment — In force from 20 February 2026 — Gazette [1] MeitY FAQ and PIB summary — Explanatory material; not a replacement for the Gazette — FAQ [4], PIB [3] Broader AI consultation paper — Not located in official sources checked; timetable reported as ministerial expectation — News on AIR [7], MediaNama [8]
Decision path for a media item
View data Step — Question 1 — Is it audio, visual or audiovisual information? 2 — Does it meet the rule’s realism and depiction test? 3 — Does a conditional exclusion apply? 4 — Is it unlawful/prohibited, or permissible with labelling and provenance duties? 5 — Which intermediary role and notice/complaint route apply?
Two clocks, two triggers
View data Clock — Trigger — Scope 3 hours — Qualifying government intimation or court order under the specified rule — Specified removal/action route; not every user report [1] 2 hours — Complaint under the separate grievance provision — Listed sensitive categories; the exact rule and complaint conditions apply [1][4]
What the notified rules actually cover The amendment adds SGI to the 2021 IT Rules. The definition covers audio, visual or audiovisual information altered using a computer resource so it appears real and depicts a person or event as indistinguishable, or likely to be perceived as indistinguishable, from a natural person or real-world event. The operative text—not a headline’s use of “deepfake”—sets the boundary. [1] The definition concerns specified media, not every model use. The Gazette excludes some transformations if they do not materially alter or misrepresent the source: routine editing, technical correction, transcription and compression. It also excludes specified document, education, research and training preparation if it does not create a false record. Accessibility and translation improvements are excluded only when they do not manipulate a material part of the media. These are conditional, not blanket, exemptions. [1] Intermediaries must take appropriate technical measures against SGI that violates applicable law. Permissible SGI is subject to prominent labelling and permanent metadata or another appropriate provenance mechanism, to the extent technically feasible. The final Gazette does not carry forward the 2025 draft’s fixed “10% of the display” or “first 10% of audio” formula. The earlier draft is context, not current law. [1][5][6] Significant social media intermediaries (SSMIs) have additional duties: user declarations about whether uploads are SGI, plus reasonable and proportionate technical measures to verify declarations and ensure the required declaration or label is present. These are intermediary duties, not a single set of obligations shared by every creator or user. [1][2] Two clocks, two triggers The phrase “three-hour takedown rule” can obscure the trigger. Under the amended Rule 3(1)(d), the three-hour window follows a qualifying intimation from the appropriate government or a court order. It is not a timer for every user report about AI-generated media. [1] A separate grievance route sets two hours for listed sensitive categories under Rule 3(2)(b). MeitY’s FAQ gives an unlawful morphed intimate image as an example, but says it does not replace or amend the Act or Rules. The category and complaint conditions still matter. [1][4] Decision guide: Is the material audio, visual or audiovisual? Does it meet the rule’s realism test? Does a conditional exclusion apply? Is it unlawful or otherwise prohibited, or permissible but subject to labelling/provenance duties? Which intermediary is involved? Which exact notice or complaint trigger applies? Each answer changes the next step; “AI-made” alone does not answer all of them. The paper is not the law The consultation-paper story is separate. News on AIR’s 8 October report attributed to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw an expectation that a paper would appear within about a month. MediaNama’s 26 October report attributed “in the coming weeks” to his remarks at the NDTV World Summit. Neither report is the paper itself or changes the February rules. [7][8] The 2025 draft shows why status labels matter. It included a specific 10% marking formula; the final Gazette used different wording. An official draft is still a proposal, not an operative rule. [1][5][6] For the wider consultation, the safe description is that the minister was reported as expecting a paper. A consultation would not by itself amend the IT Rules. Check the official document and process before updating this account. [1][2][7][8] What the record supports—and what it does not Claim — Evidence — Assessment The 2026 SGI amendment is in force. — G.S.R. 120(E) says it took effect on 20 February 2026. [1] — Supported. Every AI-generated text post is SGI. — The definition covers audio, visual or audiovisual information and applies a realism test. [1] — Not supported by this definition. Every AI media complaint has a three-hour takedown clock. — The three-hour change concerns specified government/court intimations; a distinct two-hour route addresses listed sensitive categories. [1][4] — Overbroad. The final rule mandates a fixed 10% watermark. — That formula appears in the 2025 draft, not in the final Gazette text. [1][5][6] — Not supported. A broader AI consultation paper was published by 31 October. — The reports describe expected timing; no official paper was located in this check. [7][8] — Not established by the checked sources. What this means for… Platforms and trust-and-safety teams: Separate the qualifying government/court intimation from the user-grievance route. Record the trigger, receipt time, action and escalation; map each workflow to the exact clause with qualified legal review. Creators, publishers and accessibility teams: The exclusions depend on not materially altering or misrepresenting the underlying media. Retain source files and edit notes where a transformation could be mistaken for a synthetic depiction. A disclosure does not make unlawful content lawful. Indian AI startups: Distinguish realistic-media features from general text generation, and intermediary duties from provider or user responsibilities. If a service enables publication, determine its role and the applicable technical controls. Treat a future consultation as an opportunity to comment, not as a binding deadline. What we don’t know yet 1. What exact text, scope and questions will appear in the broader AI-governance consultation paper? 2. When will the paper be issued, and what response period or consultation process will accompany it? 3. How will MeitY or courts interpret difficult boundary cases involving material alteration, synthetic media, accessibility and technical feasibility? 4. What implementation evidence will show how intermediaries apply the distinct three-hour and two-hour processes? What to watch next If MeitY publishes the paper: verify the official date, consultation deadline and whether it proposes new duties or only seeks feedback. When platforms update their policies: compare each stated procedure with the operative rule rather than assuming a company help page restates the law. If a court or ministry issues guidance: check whether it changes interpretation, describes enforcement, or merely summarizes existing requirements. At the next editorial update: replace the “paper not located” note only after checking the official document itself. FAQ Is India’s AI consultation paper already law? No. The timetable reported by news outlets is an expectation attributed to the IT minister. A consultation paper is a policy document, not automatically a binding amendment. The 2026 IT Rules amendment is a separate, notified instrument already in force. Do the rules cover every AI-generated text? The SGI definition in the notified amendment covers audio, visual or audiovisual information meeting a realism test. It does not define every AI-generated text response as SGI. Other laws or rules may still apply to particular text, conduct or services. Is every deepfake complaint subject to a three-hour deadline? No. The three-hour change applies to a specified process following a qualifying government or court intimation. The amendment also sets a separate two-hour route for listed sensitive categories of grievances. The trigger and category must be checked against the applicable clause. Did the final rules keep the 10% watermark requirement? The 10% surface-area and audio-duration formula appears in MeitY’s 2025 draft. It is not stated in the same way in the final February 2026 Gazette text, which uses a prominent-labelling standard and provenance requirements, subject to the operative wording for the relevant actors and content. Does the MeitY FAQ replace the Gazette? No. MeitY says the FAQ is explanatory and does not replace, amend or alter the IT Act or Rules. For the legal text, use the notified Gazette amendment and the consolidated Rules; the ministry expressly directs readers to the notified Rules for legal compliance. Sources Tier 1 — primary 1. input.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026: Agents Start 40% of PRs
input.dek: GitHub says agents started over 40% of September PRs. What the signal measures, misses, and how teams can track review outcomes.
input.author: global-ai-news-editorial-desk
input.body:
The bottom line GitHub’s 2026 Octoverse report says that more than 40% of pull requests on its platform started with an agent’s first draft in September, compared with 17% in March. It counts a detectable event: an agent appears to have supplied the first draft. GitHub calls the measure a floor because some agent use may not be detected. It does not tell readers what share of code was generated, how much humans rewrote, or whether merged changes were correct, secure or maintainable. The report’s two-week merge figures are a comparison of observed repository activity, not a quality test. Teams should treat the headline as a reason to inspect their review system—not proof that agents have replaced developers or that the resulting code is safe. [1] Key facts at a glance GitHub published Octoverse 2026 on 28 October, using activity through September 2026. [1] More than 40% of September pull requests started with an agent’s first draft; the reported March figure was 17%. [1][9] GitHub reports 110 million agent-started pull requests in September, about six times March’s volume. [1] The share is detection-based; GitHub describes it as a floor, not a complete count of all AI assistance. [1] Among merged pull requests with detected AI involvement, GitHub reports 44.1% for TypeScript, 41.1% for Python, 40.4% for Rust and 21.2% for Java over the 12 months checked. [1] Agent-started pull requests more often changed multiple files: about 87%, compared with 79% for pull requests without detected agent involvement. [1] By September, 90% of agent-started pull requests had merged within two weeks, versus about 86% in the comparison group. [1] GitHub’s own guidance says generated changes still need careful human review and testing before merge. [2][3] What happened: a narrow series, not a universal adoption curve Date — GitHub’s reported measure — What it supports March 2026 — 17% of pull requests started with an agent’s first draft. — A baseline in GitHub’s own platform data. [1] February 2026 — 83% of agent-involved pull requests merged within two weeks, compared with roughly 86% without detected agent involvement. — A separate measure; the groups were close, with the agent group slightly lower. [1] September 2026 — More than 40% of pull requests started with an agent’s first draft; 110 million in volume. — A later platform snapshot, not a forecast for all software development. [1] September 2026 — 90% of agent-started pull requests merged within two weeks, compared with about 86% for the comparison group. — A merge-timing statistic, not a code-quality or security score. [1] The sequence is important. The 17% and “more than 40%” figures concern the detected share of pull requests that began with an agent first draft. The two-week figures concern whether a pull request merged during a time window. They are related signals in the same report, but they do not measure the same thing and cannot be combined into a single “AI productivity” score. Original visuals Detected agent-started pull requests
View data Month — Share reported by GitHub March 2026 — 17% September 2026 — More than 40% Source: GitHub Octoverse 2026. The line joins two reported snapshots only; it does not imply monthly values or a continuous trend.
Agent-started and comparison-group outcomes
View data Language — Merged pull requests with detected AI involvement TypeScript — 44.1% Python — 41.1% Rust — 40.4% Java — 21.2% Source: GitHub Octoverse 2026, reported for the 12 months preceding publication. These percentages use a different measure from the share of pull requests started by an agent.
Agent-started and comparison-group outcomes
View data Measure, September 2026 — Agent-started — No detected agent involvement Changed multiple files — About 87% — About 79% Merged within two weeks — 90% — About 86% Source: GitHub Octoverse 2026. These are descriptive group comparisons, not proof that agent use caused the difference.
A review path, not an automatic merge
View data Stage — Evidence to inspect Agent proposal — Diff, task context, changed files Automated checks — Tests, security scans, workflow permissions Human review — Correctness, scope, dependencies, maintainability Approval — Required reviewers and branch rules Merge — CI status and repository policy The stages are an editorial workflow model informed by GitHub’s review and branch-protection documentation, not a measured Octoverse funnel. [2][3][4][5]
What 40% means—and what it does not It does mean — It does not mean In GitHub’s September platform data, more than four in ten pull requests met its detected agent-started definition. — More than four in ten lines of code were written by AI. A coding agent supplied the first draft for that detected group. — Every later edit was written by the agent or left unchanged by a human. The platform saw about 110 million such pull requests in September. — The same share applies to every company, code host, programming language or country. GitHub says the measure is a floor because it may not detect all agent use. — The metric is a complete census of AI use or a quality score. Keep the denominator attached to the number. “40%” without “of GitHub pull requests,” the September period and GitHub’s first-draft detection rule makes a narrow measure sound universal. The distinction also matters when an organization compares this figure with internal telemetry. A repository that logs accepted suggestions is counting something different from a platform that looks for an agent-created first draft. [1] What the measure counts—and leaves out GitHub describes an agent-started pull request as one whose first draft came from a coding agent that GitHub can detect. That definition is narrower than “a pull request touched by AI.” A developer may ask a model for suggestions, manually write code based on them, or use a tool whose activity does not create a detectable agent-started draft. Those cases may not appear in the measure. Conversely, a pull request that begins with an agent draft may later be substantially rewritten by a person. [1] That distinction changes the headline’s meaning. “More than 40%” is not a finding that agents authored 40% of GitHub’s code, that 40% of every developer’s work is automated, or that 40% of pull requests are accepted without human edits. It is a platform-specific share of pull requests meeting GitHub’s detection rule. The word “started” matters: it marks an entry point into the workflow, not the final distribution of authorship. GitHub’s “floor” language also matters. It signals that the platform does not claim to observe every kind of agent involvement. Readers should preserve that limitation when comparing the percentage with a company’s internal metrics or another platform’s survey. Different systems may count prompts, generated lines, accepted suggestions, agent-created branches or pull requests. Without a shared definition and denominator, percentages that all say “AI use” are not directly comparable. [1] Merge speed is not a quality score The September result that 90% of agent-started pull requests merged within two weeks can sound like an endorsement. The comparison group’s roughly 86% figure is close, and GitHub reports a different relationship earlier in the year: 83% of agent-involved pull requests merged within two weeks in February, slightly below the roughly 86% comparison rate. This is a descriptive change over time. It does not establish why the groups differed or whether the code was better. [1] A merge can reflect many things: a small patch, a routine dependency update, a strong reviewer, a permissive repository policy, or a team that prioritizes throughput. The report’s two-week measure does not by itself disclose review minutes, defect rates, rollback frequency, vulnerability findings, downstream maintenance cost or whether a merge was later reverted. Those are different outcomes and need their own data. The multi-file statistic raises another review question. GitHub says agent-started pull requests changed multiple files more often than the comparison group—about 87% versus 79%. A wider change can be sensible, but it can also make reasoning about scope and interactions harder. The percentage does not say whether those files were tightly related, whether tests covered them, or how many reviewers examined them. It should prompt teams to make review scope visible, not to treat multi-file work as inherently good or bad. [1] GitHub also reports a separate language view: among merged pull requests with detected AI involvement over the preceding 12 months, the shares were 44.1% for TypeScript, 41.1% for Python, 40.4% for Rust and 21.2% for Java. These are not the same as the share of pull requests that began with an agent. The language metric concerns merged pull requests carrying a detected AI signal; the March-to-September measure concerns agent-started first drafts. The report does not establish that the language itself caused AI involvement or that the figures represent every repository using those languages. [1] The language chart is useful as a prompt for better instrumentation, not as a ranking of languages or developers. A codebase’s age, project mix, repository visibility, team practices and detection coverage could all affect what appears in platform data. The figures should not be used to conclude that a language is “AI-native,” that its code is easier to review, or that one language’s developers need fewer reviewers. The review bottleneck is a team-level question If agents increase the rate at which draft changes appear, teams need to know whether their review capacity, tests and ownership rules can keep pace. Octoverse does not measure a universal bottleneck: it reports platform activity, not every team’s queue or reviewer workload. The practical question for an engineering manager is local. Are pull requests waiting longer? Are reviewers handling larger changes? Are defects or reversions changing? Do teams have a reliable way to identify agent involvement in their own repositories? Start with a baseline rather than borrowing GitHub’s percentage. Define the unit—a pull request, commit, generated line or accepted suggestion—then state the detection method, period and denominator. Separate agent-started changes from human-authored changes that received AI assistance. Track review latency, time to merge, review comments, test failures, post-merge defects and reversions as distinct measures. Do not collapse them into one productivity score. Teams can also make review more consistent without treating the model as a special contributor that receives less scrutiny. GitHub documents ways to require human approvals on protected branches and describes human review and testing as necessary for agent-generated changes. NIST’s secure software and AI risk frameworks provide broader process references; they do not validate this Octoverse metric or prove that a particular workflow improves outcomes. [2][3][4][5][6][7] A worked example for a repository The following numbers are hypothetical and demonstrate the calculation only. Suppose a team has 200 pull requests in one month, with 80 marked agent-started under a documented detection rule. If 64 of those 80 merge within 14 days, the team’s agent-started two-week merge rate is 64 ÷ 80 = 80%. If 96 of the remaining 120 pull requests merge within 14 days, the comparison rate is 96 ÷ 120 = 80%. That result would say the two groups had the same observed merge rate in that period. It would not say they were equally correct, secure or maintainable. The team should publish the count alongside the rate, include the observation window, state how reopened or abandoned pull requests are handled, and track later defects separately. A small denominator can move sharply when only a few pull requests change status, so counts matter as much as percentages. Do not compare that local result directly with GitHub’s 90% and 86% unless the internal team uses compatible definitions, observation windows and inclusion rules. GitHub reports an aggregate platform comparison; a single repository is a different population. The purpose of the worked example is to make a local measurement reproducible, not to reproduce GitHub’s published rate. What the record supports—and what it doesn’t Claim — Evidence — Assessment More than 40% of September pull requests began with agent first drafts. — GitHub’s October 2026 report and GitGuardian’s summary. [1][9] — Supported as a GitHub-reported, detection-based statistic. Agents wrote more than 40% of all code on GitHub. — The statistic counts detected agent-started pull requests, not code lines or total authorship. [1] — Not supported. Agent-started pull requests merged faster in September. — 90% merged within two weeks versus about 86% in the comparison group. [1] — Supported as a descriptive time-window comparison; causation and quality are not established. Agent-started pull requests changed multiple files more often. — About 87% versus 79% in the comparison group. [1] — Supported as a reported descriptive comparison. The September merge figures prove agent code is safer or better. — The cited report does not provide a code-quality, vulnerability or maintenance measure for that claim. [1] — Not established. What this means for… Engineering leaders: Use the figures to ask whether your review system is keeping up, not to set an adoption target. Establish one internal definition of agent involvement, then report the denominator, period and detection method alongside every percentage. Developers and reviewers: The first draft is only the start of review. Inspect the full diff, tests, dependencies and behavior at system boundaries. A quick merge is not a substitute for understanding what changed or why. Security teams: Check that agent-created pull requests receive the same relevant security checks as other changes. Review workflow permissions separately from code content: GitHub’s documentation warns that untrusted pull-request content can create risks when privileged Actions workflows are configured unsafely. [5] Indian IT-services firms and GCCs: The global platform number does not estimate Indian hiring or delivery changes. A firm can measure the task mix and review load of its own repositories, but should not infer staffing outcomes from GitHub’s detection metric. What we don’t know yet 1. How much human editing happens between an agent’s first draft and the merged pull request? 2. What are the defect, vulnerability, rollback and maintenance outcomes for the two groups? 3. How much agent involvement does GitHub’s detection rule miss, and does detection vary by repository or tool? 4. How do the results differ between public and private repositories? GitHub did not provide a public/private split in the passages checked. 5. How do language, repository size and project type affect the detected AI-involvement figures? What to watch next In the next Octoverse update: whether GitHub publishes its detection method, denominator details and comparable quality outcomes. When teams report internal adoption: whether they distinguish agent-started pull requests from AI-assisted human work. During repository reviews: whether required approvals, automated checks and reviewer ownership scale with change volume. If the merge-rate comparison is reused: whether the speaker preserves the time window and avoids calling it a safety or productivity result. FAQ Does “40% of pull requests” mean AI wrote 40% of all code? No. GitHub says more than 40% of September pull requests started with an agent’s first draft under its detection method. The report does not measure the share of code lines generated by AI, the amount of later human editing, or all AI assistance that may not appear as an agent-started pull request. What does GitHub mean by an agent-started pull request? GitHub describes it as a pull request whose first draft came from a coding agent that the platform can detect. That is a narrower category than any pull request where a developer used AI. It also says the metric is a floor because some agent use may not be detected. Do the merge figures show that agent code is better? No. The report says 90% of agent-started pull requests merged within two weeks in September, compared with about 86% for pull requests without detected agent involvement. That is a descriptive timing comparison, not a measure of correctness, security, maintainability or later defects. How should an engineering team measure its own agent use? Choose one unit and state the denominator, period and detection method. Keep agent-started work separate from human-authored work assisted by a model. Track merge timing, review effort, test failures and post-merge defects as separate outcomes; do not infer quality from throughput alone. Should agent-created pull requests get a different review standard? The cited GitHub guidance recommends human review and testing before agent-generated changes merge, and repository owners can configure required approvals and checks. Teams should set policies based on risk and repository controls, not assume that an agent label makes a change safer or more dangerous by itself. Sources Tier 1 — primary 1. input.title: Gemini 4 Carbon: Who Can Test It—and What Scores Show
input.dek: Google will gate Gemini 4 Carbon to cyber defenders first. We separate access claims, benchmark methods, independent results and missing safety documents.
input.author: global-ai-news-editorial-desk
input.body:
The bottom line Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon on 28 October as a frontier model for cybersecurity and long-horizon work. The company says a subset of cyber defenders will receive access first, followed by additional trusted partners through Fairwind, then developers, businesses and consumers through product surfaces “as soon as possible.” It gave no public date for that wider release. Google has published a Carbon evaluation-methodology page, so this is not a case where every claim is undocumented. But the headline security scores have different origins: Google self-computed SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym; CWE-bench uses a public leaderboard evaluated by Collinear AI; Artificial Analysis separately reports its Intelligence Index score. Limited general access makes some independent reproduction harder, not impossible for every metric. Readers should assess each result by its method, access and source—not treat the figures as one comparable safety score. Key facts at a glance Google announced Carbon on 28 October, about two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon’s release. [1] Google describes Carbon as aimed at cybersecurity defense and long-horizon capabilities. That is the company’s positioning, not an independent capability verdict. [1] Initial access is for a subset of cyber defenders; Google says it will gradually add trusted partners through Fairwind, then offer the model through product surfaces “as soon as possible.” No public date was given. [1] Google reports 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% on ExploitGym and 71.0% on CWE-bench. These are different tests with different provenance. [1][2] Google’s methodology page says it self-computed SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym; CWE-bench results come from the public leaderboard evaluated across models by Collinear AI. [2] Artificial Analysis reports a score of 59 on its Intelligence Index v5. That third-party index is not one of Google’s specialized cybersecurity benchmarks. [3] The current Fairwind page documents controls for Gemini 4 Argon. Its partner count and access requirements should not be assumed to describe Carbon’s specific admission terms. [4] Google’s official Gemini page links an Argon Safety & Security Report; a Carbon evaluation-methodology page is public, but no Carbon-specific model card or safety report was located in official pages checked on 31 October. [2][5][6] A staged access path
View data Stage — Google's stated audience — Timing in the 28 October announcement 1 — A subset of cyber defenders — Starting the week of the announcement 2 — Additional trusted partners through Fairwind — Gradual expansion; no dated schedule 3 — Developers, businesses and consumers through product surfaces — “As soon as possible”; no public date Source: Google DeepMind announcement. The announcement does not publish Carbon-specific application criteria or a general availability date. [1]
Carbon’s rollout is the story’s immediate news. Google says it is participating in the U.S. government’s voluntary pre-release testing process, will begin with a subset of cyber defenders, and will expand through trusted partners before product access. Those steps describe a sequence, not a commitment that every named audience will receive access on a particular date. [1] “Fairwind” also needs careful attribution. Google’s Fairwind page currently says that the program works with more than 650 partners and describes background checks, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, access controls, and limits on redistribution. But the page describes access to Gemini 4 Argon and its use in internal cybersecurity, incident response or penetration-testing teams. It is evidence about the program’s published Argon terms—not proof that the same exact conditions already govern Carbon. [4] The Carbon announcement does not provide a public application checklist, list of selected Carbon partners, or a date for general product access. It says Google is gathering feedback and iterating on guardrails before opening access through its product surfaces. The access ladder therefore has a clear order but incomplete operational detail. [1] The scores are not one leaderboard
View data Reported result — Figure — Provenance disclosed in checked sources SEC-bench Pro — 88.2% — Google says it self-computed the result using the open-source setup. ExploitGym — 54.8% — Google says it self-computed the result using the open-source setup. CWE-bench v1 — 71.0% — Google says results are from the public leaderboard evaluated across models by Collinear AI. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 — 59 — Artificial Analysis reports its own score; this is a general capability index, not a security benchmark. Do not compare these percentages as if they shared a test, task set or scoring method. The 59 is an index score, not a percentage.
Google’s launch post describes the external cybersecurity evaluations as run “without guardrails.” Its detailed methodology adds important distinctions. SEC-bench Pro was self-computed by Google on a 183-task JavaScript-engine split, using three independent attempts per task and the Antigravity harness. ExploitGym was also self-computed; the page describes a single attempt per task, no internet access and mitigations off, with default and extended timeouts. These settings are part of the reported evaluation—not a general description of how Carbon is deployed to users. [1][2] CWE-bench has a different origin. Google says its score comes from the public leaderboard, where Collinear AI evaluated the models. That is outside evaluation, not the same kind of Google-run result as SEC-bench Pro or ExploitGym. Artificial Analysis offers another external reference: it reports a 59 on its Intelligence Index v5. The index covers broader model capabilities and cannot validate the specialized security scores. [2][3] The article should not say “no outside lab has tested Carbon.” That would overstate the case. A public third-party index score exists, and the CWE-bench result is described as an evaluation by Collinear AI. The narrower question is whether outsiders can reproduce each particular security result under the same conditions, with access to the same model version, settings and task data. The pages checked do not establish independent reproduction of Google’s self-computed SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym figures. [2][3] What a benchmark means when access is limited A benchmark number is conditional on its test set, scoring rule, model version, prompt or harness, tools, time limit, attempts and safety settings. “88.2%” does not tell a reader what counts as a success until those details are known. Google’s methodology page supplies more information than a launch headline alone, including which results are self-computed and which draw on third-party evaluations. That transparency helps readers ask sharper questions, but does not turn all reported figures into independently reproduced results. [1][2] The no-guardrails disclosure also needs a boundary. It identifies the setup used for the external cybersecurity evaluations. It does not establish that consumer-facing Carbon will be released without safeguards, or that the model’s runtime policy is absent. Google’s launch post says it is iterating on guardrails during the staged rollout. A benchmark condition and a product deployment condition are separate facts. [1][2] Use this checklist when a vendor publishes a capability score: 1. Name the exact model and version. Does the benchmark page identify the tested model, settings and evaluation date? 2. Check who ran it. Is the result computed by the vendor, a benchmark maintainer, an external evaluator, or a leaderboard that aggregates submissions? 3. Inspect the task set and scoring rule. What is the denominator? What qualifies as a pass? Are results averaged across attempts? 4. Record the conditions. Note tools, access to the internet, mitigations or guardrails, timeout, reasoning settings and whether test-time compute is limited. 5. Check comparison fairness. Were competing models tested on the same tasks, versions, harnesses and dates, or copied from separate reports? 6. Look for replication. Can another lab access the model and reproduce the same result? If not, distinguish a published method from a reproduced result. 7. Keep the claim narrow. A benchmark result supports performance on that task under those conditions—not overall security, safety or real-world operational success. The checklist is a reporting method, not a claim that any single benchmark is useless. Tests can provide valuable evidence. They become misleading when a precise number is detached from its measurement design or treated as a complete account of a system. NIST’s Generative AI Profile is a risk-management reference, not a benchmark or an evaluation of Carbon. Its role here is to reinforce that capability measurements sit within a broader process of identifying and managing risks; it cannot validate any of the figures above. [9] Access approaches: related controls, different jobs
View data Example — What is controlled — What the public source says — Boundary Gemini 4 Carbon — External access to a frontier model — Selected cyber defenders first, then trusted partners, followed by broader product access without a public date. [1] — Carbon-specific vetting and dates are not detailed in the announcement. Fairwind / Gemini 4 Argon — Partner access and use — Google documents due diligence, phishing-resistant MFA, internal security-team limits and non-redistribution. [4] — The page names Argon; do not transfer its exact requirements to Carbon without confirmation. OpenAI frontier training environment — Isolation of model training infrastructure — OpenAI says it paused training after a DNS resolver misconfiguration, resumed in an offline environment and describes the containment measures. [7] — Training-environment isolation is not a public model access program.
Access restriction and training containment solve different problems. Fairwind controls which organizations and teams can use a model under specified terms. OpenAI’s October account concerns the environment used to train frontier models after an infrastructure misconfiguration; OpenAI said it resumed training offline. Neither type of control proves a model’s benchmark claims, and an offline training setup does not tell a user who can access a released model. [4][7] This distinction matters for organizations making a procurement or security decision. Ask separately: who can access the model; what controls apply to that access; what system documentation is public; and who can test the model independently? A vendor may answer one question clearly while leaving another open. The current record answers Carbon’s high-level access order and benchmark methodology more clearly than it answers Carbon-specific partner admission criteria or broad release timing. [1][2][4] A timeline: Argon, then Carbon
View data Date — Event 13 October 2026 — Gemini 4 Argon reached developers, according to the official Google launch chronology. [8] 28 October 2026 — Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon and staged access. [1] 31 October 2026 — This draft’s official-page check found a Carbon evaluation-methodology page, an Argon model card and Argon safety report, but no Carbon model card or Carbon-specific safety report. [2][5][6] The Carbon general-access date remains unspecified in the announcement. [1]
Google’s Carbon page now has a public evaluation-methodology document. The checked Gemini model page links to a Gemini 4 Argon model card and a Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report. A direct Carbon model-card URL checked on 31 October returned 404; that response is a point-in-time check, not proof that a page will not be published later. The precise statement is that no Carbon-specific model card or safety report was found on the official pages checked by this draft’s update time. [2][5][6] Carbon’s introductory API price—$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens—is also public in the announcement. Price is not availability: the company did not attach a public access date to that price. The distinction is useful for business planning because a listed rate does not establish that a team can sign up, test the model or rely on a production service. [1] What the record supports—and what it does not Claim — Evidence — Assessment Google announced Carbon and staged access on 28 October. — Google DeepMind announcement. [1] — Supported as a vendor announcement. Carbon is already broadly available to developers. — Google says defenders and trusted partners first; wider product access will follow “as soon as possible.” [1] — Not supported by the announcement checked. Google reports 88.2% SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% ExploitGym and 71.0% CWE-bench. — Launch post and evaluation page. [1][2] — Supported as reported figures; provenance differs by benchmark. No one outside Google has evaluated Carbon. — Artificial Analysis publishes an Index v5 result; Collinear AI evaluated CWE-bench across models. [2][3] — Not supported. The 59 Artificial Analysis score confirms Google’s security results. — It is a general capability index, separate from SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym and CWE-bench. [2][3] — Not supported. Fairwind’s 650+ partner count and published Argon terms apply unchanged to Carbon. — The checked Fairwind page describes Argon access. [4] — Not established for Carbon. Carbon has no public documentation. — Google’s Carbon evaluation-methodology page is public. [2] — Too broad. The precise gap is the lack of a Carbon-specific model card or safety report located in this check. What this means for… Security teams: A restricted model can be useful for controlled evaluation, but request the exact version, access conditions, test settings, data handling terms and incident contacts. Do not treat Google’s reported score as a substitute for an evaluation against your own defensive tasks and policies. Startups that depend on APIs: The introductory rate is not a launch date or service commitment. Keep architecture and cost assumptions flexible until the model is actually available under documented terms. Verify rate limits, data retention, uptime commitments and the distinction between preview and production access. Regulators and evaluators: Separate capability claims from access rules and safety documentation. A published evaluation method helps scrutiny; independent replication requires suitable access, stable versions and enough task detail to reproduce outcomes. The Carbon case shows why a general index, a public leaderboard and a vendor-run benchmark should be reported as different evidence. Researchers and benchmark maintainers: Record when a vendor uses a public leaderboard, a self-computed harness or an external index. Preserve version, evaluator and settings metadata so future comparisons do not silently combine unlike runs. What we don’t know yet 1. Which organizations have been selected for Carbon’s first defender group, and what Carbon-specific vetting requirements apply? 2. When will Carbon become available to developers, businesses or consumers through a public product surface? 3. Will Google publish a Carbon-specific model card or Safety & Security Report, and how will it describe safety evaluations? 4. Can independent researchers reproduce the SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym results with the same model version and test conditions? 5. How do real defensive deployments perform after accounting for false positives, human review, patch quality and operational constraints? What to watch next If Google updates Fairwind materials: check whether the page names Carbon and states Carbon-specific participant, authentication and redistribution requirements. If Carbon reaches a public surface: record the version, date, terms, rate limits and whether the released model matches the evaluated version. If a Carbon safety report or model card appears: compare the documented safety scope with the existing evaluation-methodology page; do not substitute one document for the other. If a new benchmark result is reported: identify who ran it and whether its method is independent, public or vendor-computed. If Google changes the launch price: record the effective date and distinguish introductory rates from standard pricing. FAQ Is Gemini 4 Carbon available to everyone? No public general-availability date was stated in Google’s 28 October announcement. Google said a subset of cyber defenders would receive access first, then additional trusted partners through Fairwind, followed by developers, businesses and consumers through product surfaces “as soon as possible.” The announcement describes a staged sequence, not a public signup date. Are Google’s cybersecurity benchmark results independently verified? Not all in the same way. Google says it self-computed the SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym results. It says CWE-bench comes from the public leaderboard evaluated by Collinear AI. Artificial Analysis reports a separate general capability index score. These sources provide different kinds of evidence and do not establish identical independent reproduction for each benchmark. Does “without guardrails” mean Carbon will ship without safeguards? No. Google says its external cybersecurity evaluations were run without guardrails, and separately says it is iterating on guardrails during the staged rollout. Evaluation conditions describe how a test was run; they do not by themselves establish the safeguards in a future product deployment. Does Fairwind’s published MFA requirement apply to Carbon? The Fairwind page checked for this draft describes controls for Gemini 4 Argon, including phishing-resistant MFA, background checks and restrictions on which teams may use the model. The Carbon announcement refers to staged Fairwind access but does not state that every Argon-specific condition already applies to Carbon. Wait for Carbon-specific terms before assuming they are identical. Is the 59 Artificial Analysis score a cybersecurity score? No. Artificial Analysis calls it an Intelligence Index v5 score, a broader capability measure. It is separate from SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym and CWE-bench. It provides an external evaluation reference, but it cannot validate or replace the specialized cybersecurity results for those separate tasks. Sources Tier 1 — primary / independent evaluation 1. input.title: Anthropic S-1: Who Owns It—and Who Controls the Board?
input.dek: Anthropic’s S-1 separates public economic rights from founder voting power and Trust board control. We explain the proposed classes and reported loss.
input.author: global-ai-news-editorial-desk
input.body:
The bottom line Anthropic’s 26 October Form S-1 describes a proposed listing in which public investors could buy Class A shares with economic rights without controlling the board. The filing proposes two separate governance levers: a single Class F share held by the founders’ LLC would carry 50.1% of voting power on matters submitted to shareholders generally, including the election of directors other than the Class T directors; and the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), through a Class T share, would generally elect and remove the Class T directors, who together would make up a majority of the authorized board. Both special classes have no economic rights, according to the filing. These terms are proposals in a registration statement, not a completed offering. Anthropic has not announced a price range, share count or offering date. [1][2] The structure separates three questions that are often collapsed into “who owns the company?”: who receives economic value, who votes on ordinary shareholder matters, and who can choose the board. The S-1 answers them differently. It does not establish how the structure will work in every future dispute, whether the Trust will exercise its powers in a particular way, or what public Class A shareholders will earn. What the filing proposes
View data Class — Proposed holder or holders — Economic rights in the S-1 — Voting or board role described in the filing A — Public investors and other eligible holders — Yes; the proposed IPO offers Class A common stock — Ordinary shareholder voting; does not elect the Class T directors T — Long-Term Benefit Trust — None — Generally elects and removes Class T directors, who together are a majority of the authorized board; no general shareholder vote F — Founder LLC — None — One share carries 50.1% of total voting power on matters submitted to shareholders generally, including election of directors other than Class T directors E — Employees, excluding co-founders — None — Limited voting on specified matters This is a summary of proposed terms, not legal advice. See the S-1 for the full terms, exceptions and conditions. [1]
The filing says the proposed offering is for Class A common stock. It also says Anthropic intends to list the shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” That is an intention, not a completed listing. The company’s own filing announcement says the number of shares and price range had not been determined. [1][2] Class A is the economic class prospective public investors are being offered. The S-1’s special Class T and Class F shares have no economic rights. This means the Class F share’s 50.1% vote is not a statement that the founders own 50.1% of Anthropic’s economic value. Nor does it mean that public shareholders receive 49.9% of every vote: Class T has no general shareholder vote, and the filing also describes limited voting rights for Class E. The safest description is the filing’s own: Class F will hold 50.1% of the total voting power on matters submitted to shareholders generally. [1] Board selection and shareholder voting are different
View data Decision point — Proposed route in the S-1 — What it does not mean Majority of board seats — LTBT generally elects and removes the Class T directors through Class T; those directors together constitute a majority of the authorized board — It does not give the Trust economic ownership of the company Most shareholder matters — Founder LLC’s one Class F share carries 50.1% of voting power — It does not mean the founders’ LLC receives 50.1% of economic returns Public investment — Class A common stock is the security offered — It does not give Class A holders the power to elect the Class T directors Company management — The board appoints and oversees executives under the described governance structure — The S-1 does not predict the outcome of future board or shareholder disputes
The filing describes the LTBT as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in areas including AI safety, national security, public policy and social enterprise. Through Class T, the Trust generally has authority to elect and remove the Class T directors. The S-1 says that group will constitute a majority of the authorized board. In parallel, the single Class F share would be held by Founder LLC, whose initial members would be Anthropic’s seven co-founders. [1] The filing says Class F’s 50.1% voting power applies to matters submitted to shareholders generally, including election of directors other than the Class T directors. That wording is more precise than saying “the founders control every vote.” It specifies a large voting block and its stated scope, while the Trust’s Class T authority covers the separate process for selecting a majority of the board. Neither phrase alone tells readers how all future questions will be resolved. [1] The S-1 describes the relevant rights as part of a proposed post-offering structure. Class T and Class F are to be issued immediately before completion of the offering. Until the offering closes, readers should not write as if those proposed securities have already been issued under the IPO terms. The document is a registration statement: terms can be revised, and the company has not announced that the transaction is complete. [1][2] How the current filing compares with Anthropic’s 2023 explanation
View data Date — Public document — What it says 19 September 2023 — Anthropic’s LTBT announcement — Describes a trust-held Class T share and a phase-in of board appointment authority, with a majority within four years, plus an investor-elected board seat 13 July 2026 — SEC draft registration statement — Describes the governance architecture before the October S-1 26 October 2026 — SEC Form S-1 — Proposes that Class T directors will constitute a majority of the authorized board after the offering The 2023 explanation is historical context. For proposed IPO terms, the October 2026 S-1 is the controlling source. [1][3][4]
Anthropic’s 2023 announcement presented the Trust as a governance structure that would phase in over time and funding milestones, reaching a board majority within four years. It also described an investor-elected board seat. The October 2026 S-1 describes the IPO-era proposal: the Class T directors would together be a majority of the authorized board, while the Founder LLC’s Class F share would carry the specified general shareholder voting power. [1][3] The difference is important, but it is not enough by itself to claim a contradiction. The documents were published at different stages, address different financing contexts and describe powers with different timing. The 2023 post explains the arrangement at its then-current stage; the S-1 describes the structure proposed for the offering. The 2026 filing should be used for the IPO terms, and the older announcement should be labeled as historical context—not silently combined with it. [1][3][4] The S-1 also frames Anthropic’s public-benefit purpose as the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. Delaware’s public-benefit corporation statute requires directors to balance stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the interests of people materially affected by the corporation’s conduct, and the public benefit identified in the certificate. PBC status does not mean the company is a charity, that returns no longer matter, or that the public benefit automatically overrides every other consideration. [1][5] The financial figures are not one story about profitability
View data Period or measure — Figure in the S-1 — Important boundary FY2025 revenue — $4.6 billion — Full fiscal year H1 2025 revenue — $1.2 billion — Six months ended 30 June 2025 H1 2026 revenue — $16.3 billion — Six months ended 30 June 2026 H1 2026 operating loss — $693 million — Operating result before non-operating items H1 2026 net loss — $80.7 billion — Includes a $72.4 billion change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs Top-five customer concentration — Approximately 25% of revenue — Nine months ended 30 September 2026, not H1 Issuer-reported amounts from the S-1; rounded for readability. [1]
The filing reports $4.6 billion in revenue for 2025 and $16.3 billion for the six months ended 30 June 2026, compared with $1.2 billion in the comparable 2025 half. It separately reports an operating loss of $693 million and a net loss of $80.7 billion for H1 2026. The gap between those two loss measures is material: the S-1 reports a $72.4 billion change in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, with most of the change attributed to the increased fair value of convertible promissory notes as the company’s enterprise valuation increased. [1] That is not the same as a $72.4 billion cash operating expense. It is a reported fair-value change in financing instruments. A headline that says simply “Anthropic lost $80.7 billion” is technically tied to the filing’s net-loss line but hides the accounting composition. A headline that removes the fair-value change and calls Anthropic profitable would also overreach: the filing reports an operating loss and additional financial statement items. The useful comparison states both figures, the period, and the reason the net figure diverges. [1][6] Customer concentration needs the same period discipline. Anthropic says its top five customers represented approximately 25% of revenue for the nine months ended 30 September 2026. That is not a first-half figure. The filing also warns that a small number of customers account for significant revenue, a risk to monitor as the company moves toward a public offering. [1] What the S-1 supports—and what it does not
View data Claim — Filing status — Reporting treatment Class F has 50.1% of general shareholder voting power — Stated in the S-1 — Attribute to the proposed offering terms Class T directors will be a majority of the authorized board — Stated in the S-1 — Explain the Trust’s board role separately from ordinary votes H1 2026 revenue was $16.3 billion — Stated in the S-1 — Preserve the six-month period H1 2026 net loss was $80.7 billion — Stated in the S-1 — Pair with the $693 million operating loss and $72.4 billion fair-value change IPO price, share count and date — Not determined in the company’s announcement — Do not state an offering valuation or timetable “The Trust will always act in the public interest” — Not established by the filing — Do not predict trustee decisions
The company filed an S-1, which is a registration statement, not a final prospectus with a set price. Anthropic’s announcement said the share count and price range had not yet been determined. The company proposed the ticker ANT and Nasdaq listing venue; it did not set an offering date. No calculation from the financial tables can substitute for missing offering terms. [1][2][6] The S-1 can describe formal powers, but it cannot prove how trustees, founders, directors or public investors will behave in a future conflict. It cannot show what the share price will be, whether the IPO will be completed, or whether future changes to the charter will alter the structure. Those are open questions, not gaps to fill with an estimate or an assumption. [1] What this means for… Prospective investors: Read the capital structure as three separate layers—economic rights, ordinary shareholder votes and board selection. The filing proposes Class A as the IPO security, but it does not offer a price range or share count yet. A ticker reservation and S-1 filing do not reveal what the shares will cost or whether the offering is suitable for an individual investor. Employees: The S-1 also describes Class E shares for employees other than co-founders, with no economic rights and voting on limited matters. That class is distinct from Class A, T and F. The summary here does not replace the plan documents or employee disclosures that would govern a specific grant. [1] AI governance researchers: The Trust is not an abstract mission statement; the S-1 attaches board-election and removal powers to a separate class of shares. Evaluate the charter’s actual rights, transition conditions, trustee independence and amendment provisions. Then distinguish those legal mechanisms from the company’s public explanation of why it created them. Journalists: Keep the 2023 Trust explanation, the July draft registration statement and the October S-1 in their proper timeline. The current offering terms should be attributed to the current filing, while earlier descriptions can explain how the structure evolved. Do not merge figures or rights from documents filed at different dates without identifying the document. What we don’t know yet 1. What price range and number of Class A shares will Anthropic propose in an amended S-1? 2. When will the company seek to complete the offering, and will the proposed listing go ahead? 3. How will the final prospectus describe any changes to Class T, Class F, Class E or the LTBT? 4. How will the Trust and board use their powers in a real disagreement with founders or public shareholders? 5. What will the post-offering economic ownership and voting percentages be after the final share count and any concurrent transactions? What to watch next Amended registration statements: compare changes to the proposed share classes, board rights, financials and risk factors. Price range and share count: report them only after a filing or company announcement supplies the terms. Final prospectus: verify the exact class rights, exceptions, dilution and any changes to the Trust arrangement. Offering completion: distinguish filing, pricing and closing; they are separate milestones. Financial statements: keep fair-value changes, operating results and cash flows distinct, and preserve the stated reporting periods. FAQ Who controls Anthropic under the proposed S-1 structure? The filing describes separate powers. The Long-Term Benefit Trust would generally elect and remove the Class T directors, who together would be a majority of the authorized board. The founders’ LLC would hold one Class F share carrying 50.1% of voting power on matters submitted to shareholders generally. The S-1 does not reduce control to a single owner percentage. Do Anthropic’s founders own 50.1% of the company? The S-1 says one Class F share held by the Founder LLC would carry 50.1% of total voting power on matters submitted to shareholders generally. It also says Class F has no economic rights. That is a voting-power figure, not a statement that the founders own 50.1% of Anthropic’s economic value. Is Anthropic already publicly traded? No. Anthropic filed a registration statement for a proposed initial public offering and said it intended to list Class A shares on Nasdaq under ANT. The company announcement said the share count and price range had not been set. A filing and intended ticker are not the same as an IPO closing or a public market listing. Why is the reported net loss much larger than the operating loss? The S-1 reports a $693 million operating loss and an $80.7 billion net loss for H1 2026. It includes a $72.4 billion fair-value change in convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, primarily driven by an increase in the fair value of convertible promissory notes as enterprise valuation increased. A fair-value change is not the same as cash operating expense. Does public-benefit corporation status mean Anthropic can ignore shareholder returns? input.title: Hyperscaler CapEx: Why 2026 Figures Don’t Add Cleanly
input.dek: Meta, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon report different capital-spending figures. We explain the mismatched periods, lease bases and AI-only gaps.
input.author: global-ai-news-editorial-desk
input.body:
The bottom line The latest company disclosures do not support one verified four-company “AI capex” figure for 2026. Meta’s $135–145 billion guidance includes principal payments on finance leases. Alphabet’s $195–205 billion outlook is a company capital-expenditure forecast, with $51.4 billion reported for Q3 and most spending tied to technical infrastructure. Microsoft’s roughly $170 billion estimate is for calendar 2026, while its fiscal Q1 reported $45.2 billion of CapEx, including $7.4 billion in finance leases. Amazon’s 29 October Q3 release confirms approximately $220 billion in 2026 cash capital expenditures, with the majority expected to go to AWS. These figures still differ in period, accounting basis and category. None is an audited measure of AI-only investment. A combined $700–745 billion headline should therefore be withheld until the underlying rows are reconciled. The more useful question is not “How large is the total?” but “What does each company mean by capital spending, for which period, and for what kind of infrastructure?” Company filings and calls answer parts of that question. They do not supply a consistent four-company table of AI-only cash outlays. What each company has actually said
View data Company — Latest figure found — Period and basis — Verification status Meta — $135–145B — 2026; includes principal payments on finance leases — Official Q3 release Alphabet — $195–205B — 2026 guidance; Q3 CapEx was $51.4B — Official call transcript Microsoft — About $170B — Calendar 2026 estimate; FY2027 Q1 CapEx was $45.2B, including $7.4B in finance leases — Official call transcript Amazon — About $220B cash CapEx — 2026; majority for AWS — Official Q3 release; cash basis differs from other rows The amounts are not yet on a common basis and are not AI-only totals. [1–8]
Meta’s 21 October Q3 release reports $34.91 billion in quarterly capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, and maintains a $135–145 billion 2026 range on that same stated basis. That definition is unusually explicit and should travel with the number every time it is repeated. [1] Alphabet’s 28 October earnings-call transcript keeps 2026 capital-expenditure guidance at $195–205 billion. It reports $51.4 billion in Q3, with most spending directed to technical infrastructure. The transcript does not make that entire category synonymous with AI, and the basis should not be silently converted into Meta’s lease-inclusive definition. [2] Microsoft’s FY2027 Q1 call gives an estimate of approximately $170 billion for calendar 2026. The company also reports $45.2 billion of CapEx in the quarter ended 30 September, including $7.4 billion in finance leases. Its explanation for the calendar estimate points to third-party capacity deliveries delayed into the second half. That is a timing explanation, not a claim that the annual estimate fell because of lease accounting. [3] Amazon’s official 29 October Q3 release says the company continues to expect approximately $220 billion in 2026 cash capital expenditures, the majority for AWS, and expects to spend meaningfully more in 2027. This verifies the annual estimate from a primary company source; third-party call transcripts also carry similar wording. The figure is still a cash-CapEx measure, so it is not automatically comparable with Meta’s lease-inclusive range or the other companies’ capital-expenditure presentations. [4–8] Why the numbers do not add cleanly
View data Reconciliation check — Why it matters in this comparison Period — Calendar 2026 is not the same as a fiscal quarter or a fiscal-year outlook. Lease accounting — Meta includes finance-lease principal in its stated range; Microsoft identifies leases in its quarterly figure. Cash versus CapEx — Amazon’s annual figure is confirmed as cash CapEx in its official release; it is not normalized to other companies. Investment category — Technical infrastructure and total capital expenditures include equipment and facilities that may support more than AI.
Period alignment: An annual forecast and a single quarter’s actual spending answer different questions. A quarter is useful as a run-rate signal, but multiplying it by four assumes a steady pace that the companies have not promised. Microsoft’s fiscal first quarter is also not the first quarter of calendar 2026. Its calendar-year estimate is a separate forward-looking statement. [2][3] Lease treatment: Meta explicitly includes finance-lease principal in its 2026 guidance. Microsoft’s Q1 figure includes $7.4 billion in finance leases. A cash-only estimate, a CapEx measure including finance leases and a CapEx line presented under another company’s reporting convention are not automatically equivalent. A comparison needs to state which treatment it uses and whether every company reported enough detail to normalize the others. [1][3] CapEx versus cash CapEx: Amazon’s official release calls its $220 billion figure “cash capital expenditures.” That primary wording resolves the source question, but not the comparison question: cash CapEx should not be treated as interchangeable with another company’s reported capital-expenditure guidance without checking the underlying definition. The estimate can be reported as Amazon’s guidance while still being excluded from a normalized four-company total. [4–8] AI spending versus infrastructure: The company figures are not a common measure of investment solely in AI. Meta’s range covers capital spending, not a disclosed AI-only bucket. Alphabet describes most Q3 spending as technical infrastructure, which can support several services and workloads. Microsoft and Amazon discuss cloud and data-center capacity alongside AI demand, but those broad categories do not isolate an AI-only amount. A label such as “AI CapEx” would require a company-provided allocation or a carefully disclosed estimate; the current figures do not provide one. [1–4] The difference between guidance and a market estimate
View data Evidence type — Example in this report — Use Official annual guidance — Meta $135–145B; Alphabet $195–205B — Attribute to issuer and preserve basis Official call estimate — Microsoft about $170B calendar 2026 — Preserve period and stated reason Official quarterly actual — Meta $34.91B; Alphabet $51.4B; Microsoft $45.2B — Do not treat as annual guidance Official company release — Amazon about $220B cash CapEx — Primary-confirmed; preserve cash basis and do not treat as AI-only Secondary transcript/reporting — Amazon Q3 call — Corroborating context; not the primary basis for the figure Analyst or press aggregation — $700–745B combined framing — Do not repeat as AI-only or fully reconciled
There is a practical difference between a statement in a company release, a manager’s estimate on a call, a third-party transcript of that call and an analyst’s combined number. Each can be useful. They answer different evidentiary questions. A secondary transcript may preserve a sentence accurately, but an earnings release, filed transcript or primary recording is the stronger basis for a definitive company attribution. [1–8] The $700–745 billion combined framing is not used here. Amazon’s estimate is confirmed in its official release, but the four figures still mix different periods, accounting bases and categories. Even if every individual estimate is confirmed, the sum would remain total capital spending, not necessarily AI spending. A precise total can conceal a weak definition. [1–8] The companies’ own financial materials also caution that forward-looking guidance is uncertain and subject to changing conditions. This report records what management said as of the cited dates, not a forecast of final 2026 spending. Later quarterly results may revise the outlook or explain additional changes in investment timing. [1–4] A reporting table that preserves the gaps Company — Official evidence available by 31 October — What this report can say — What remains open Meta — Q3 release and 2026 guidance — $135–145B for 2026, including finance-lease principal; Q3 was $34.91B on that basis — Which portion supports AI specifically Alphabet — Q3 call transcript and results — $195–205B for 2026; Q3 CapEx $51.4B; most Q3 spend was technical infrastructure — A company-reported AI-only allocation and a fully normalized lease basis Microsoft — FY2027 Q1 call transcript and results — About $170B calendar-year 2026 estimate; Q1 $45.2B including $7.4B leases; capacity deliveries were delayed into H2 — A common cash/accrual and category basis for the four-company comparison Amazon — Q3 release and call-page audio — Official release confirms about $220B 2026 cash CapEx, majority for AWS — A definition aligned to the other companies and an AI-only allocation remain unavailable This is a reconciliation table, not a company ranking. The gaps are visible because hiding them would make the comparison less useful. A reader who wants to build a total can do so only after choosing a definition—cash spending or accounting CapEx, calendar or fiscal year, lease-inclusive or lease-exclusive—and confirming each company’s row under that definition. Quarterly actuals can help explain the pace of investment, but they cannot fill missing annual definitions. Meta’s Q3 number is reported on the same lease-inclusive basis as its annual range; the other quarterly figures still have to be read alongside each company’s own forecast and fiscal calendar. Multiplying a quarter by four would assume a steady spending pattern, ignore delivery timing, and turn an actual into an unsupported forecast. The available company sources do not justify that step. [1–3] What this means for… Data-center operators: The figures show that large infrastructure commitments are still planned across the biggest cloud and social platforms, but they do not tell a supplier which category of capacity will be purchased, where it will be deployed or how much is contracted. Avoid using the aggregate as a proxy for a specific customer pipeline. Investors and analysts: Compare the company’s own period and definition before treating a headline as an increase or decrease. Calendar-year estimates, fiscal-year guidance, cash CapEx and lease-inclusive CapEx can move in different directions. This article does not assess valuation, returns or whether any company is spending too much. Technology buyers: Broader infrastructure growth can affect cloud availability and product investment, but these public figures do not determine an individual customer’s pricing, performance or service capacity. Company-level CapEx is not an availability guarantee. Journalists: Use “capital spending” or “CapEx” when that is what the cited source reports. Use “AI spending” only when the source reports an AI-specific amount or when the estimate method and assumptions are disclosed. Keep the company, date, period and lease treatment next to the figure. What we don’t know yet 1. What specific spending categories and lease treatment sit inside Amazon’s cash-CapEx definition? 2. Will any company publish a comparable AI-only allocation or a normalized cross-company basis? 3. What share of each company’s 2026 spending is attributable exclusively to AI infrastructure? 4. Can the four companies’ estimates be normalized to the same lease, cash/accrual and calendar-year basis? 5. How will subsequent earnings updates change these 2026 guidance ranges? What to watch next Amazon’s next filing or call: check for further detail on cash CapEx, lease treatment and the AWS share. Amended guidance: record new ranges with the date and the measure each company uses. Quarterly filings: compare reported CapEx, finance leases and cash-flow statements without treating one as a substitute for another. AI-specific disclosures: only calculate an AI-only total if companies publish an allocation or the estimate method can be independently documented. 2027 planning: keep future-year estimates separate from calendar-2026 guidance and actuals. FAQ How much will the four companies spend on AI in 2026? The checked sources do not provide a consistent AI-only total. Meta, Alphabet and Microsoft report broad capital-spending guidance on different bases. Amazon’s official Q3 release confirms about $220 billion in 2026 cash CapEx, most for AWS. But that does not align the four bases or identify AI-only spending. The article therefore does not add the figures or label a sum as AI spending. Why is Meta’s $135–145 billion range not directly comparable with Microsoft’s estimate? Meta says its 2026 range includes principal payments on finance leases. Microsoft’s roughly $170 billion figure is an estimate for calendar 2026, while its fiscal Q1 CapEx was $45.2 billion including $7.4 billion in finance leases. The annual periods and reporting details differ, and the sources do not establish a fully normalized basis. What does Alphabet’s $195–205 billion guidance include? Alphabet’s Q3 call maintained a 2026 capital-expenditure range of $195–205 billion and reported $51.4 billion in Q3, with most spending directed to technical infrastructure. That company description is broader than an AI-only allocation. The available sources do not support relabeling the full range as AI spending. Is Amazon’s approximately $220 billion figure confirmed? Yes. Amazon’s official Q3 release says it expects approximately $220 billion in 2026 cash capital expenditures, with most going to AWS. That confirms Amazon’s own estimate. It does not make the figure directly comparable with the other companies’ accounting bases or turn the amount into an AI-only allocation, so the article still excludes a combined total. Why not report the combined $700–745 billion estimate? The sum mixes different periods, accounting bases and investment categories. It also combines broad capital spending, not company-reported AI-only investment. Reporting the aggregate as a verified AI total would imply a consistent definition that the checked sources do not provide. Sources Tier 1 — primary / official 1. Meta Platforms, Q3 2026 Results, 21 October 2026. https://investor.atmeta.com/investor-news/press-release-details/2026/Meta-Reports-Third-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx 2. Alphabet Investor Relations, 2026 Q3 Earnings Call, 28 October 2026. https://abc.xyz/investor/events/event-details/2026/2026-Q3-Earnings-Call-2026-Ujou16CTw9/default.aspx 3. Microsoft Investor Relations, FY2027 Q1 Earnings Conference Call, 28 October 2026. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/Investor/events/fy-2027/earnings-fy-2027-q1 4. Amazon, Q3 2026 Results, 29 October 2026. https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/amazon-earnings-q3-2026-report 5. Amazon Investor Relations, Q3 2026 Amazon.com, Inc. Earnings Conference Call, 29 October 2026; official page links audio. https://ir.aboutamazon.com/events/event-details/2026/Q3-2026-Amazoncom-Inc-Earnings-Conference-Call/default.aspx Tier 2 — secondary transcript/reporting 6. CNBC, Amazon holds 2026 capex unchanged at $220 billion, 29 October 2026. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/29/amazon-amzn-q3-earnings-report-2026.html 7. The Motley Fool, Amazon Q3 2026 earnings call transcript, 30 October 2026. https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/10/30/amazon-amzn-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript 8.
